say: First, decide which kind of dashboard you are building, because it decides almost everything else.
A strategic dashboard is for directors. A few headline numbers, usually checked monthly.

cards.d: For directors and boards. A few headline numbers like revenue and margin, usually checked monthly.
For supervisors running daily work. Today's orders, low stock, late deliveries. Checked daily or hourly.
For analysts asking why. More filters, drill-downs and detail tables to investigate a problem.

say: An operational dashboard is for supervisors running daily work, such as today's orders and late deliveries. It is checked daily or even hourly.

say: Professionals start with a short written brief, not with the tool.
For example, Ngozi spent about two days a month on a 20-page report that her managing director rarely read past page 3. So she asked him what he actually checks.

Turn that into three dashboard questions
Note the audience and how often they view
List the data each question needs

say: She turned his answer into three questions. Are we on target? Which branch is furthest behind? Which categories have fallen compared with last year?

say: She noted the audience: one director, viewing monthly, mostly on his phone. That makes it a strategic dashboard with few filters.

say: Then she listed the data needed, including at least 13 months of history, so that same month last year exists.
Here is the rule. Every visual you add must answer one of your questions. If it answers none, it does not go on the page.

say: Most business data arrives as one wide sheet, which gets huge and slow in a BI tool. So you split it into a star schema.
A fact table records events you count or add up, such as each sale line.

panel.heading: Fact tables and dimension tables
left: Events you count or add up
right: Text you filter and group by

say: A dimension table describes the things involved: branches, products, customers and dates.
In Ngozi's model, the branch name used to be stored 18,000 times. Now it is stored 4 times.

panel.heading: Fact tables and dimension tables
left: Events you count or add up
right: Text you filter and group by

say: Write down the grain: what one row of the fact table means, such as one product on one invoice. Mixing grains causes double counting.

panel.heading: Five rules for a sound model
items: Write down the grain of the fact table
Keep every dimension key unique
One-to-many, single direction filters
Build a complete date table
Keep targets in their own small table

say: Keep every dimension key unique. If product code P-104 appears twice with two spellings, its sales can be counted twice.

panel.heading: Five rules for a sound model

say: Link each dimension to the fact table with a one-to-many relationship, and keep the filter direction single, so filters flow from dimensions down to facts.

say: A calculated column is worked out once, row by row, when the data loads. Use it to group or filter, like a price band per product.
A measure is calculated when a visual asks for it, so it responds to every filter. Use measures for totals and ratios, like profit margin.
Here is the most common calculation mistake. Ngozi's director asks for the combined profit margin of two branches.
Lagos sold 4,000,000 naira with 600,000 naira profit. That is a 15% margin.
Kano sold 1,000,000 naira with 300,000 naira profit. That is 30%.
The wrong method averages the two margins and gets 22.5%.
The right method adds first, then divides. 900,000 divided by 5,000,000 is 18%.
Ratios must be sum divided by sum, never an average of ratios. Test every new measure in a plain table with a calculator before you chart it.
To remember. Write your questions and audience down first. Facts hold events, dimensions hold descriptions.
Keep keys unique and your date table complete. Use measures for anything that must respond to filters, and calculate ratios as sum divided by sum.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Write questions and audience before you build
Facts hold events; dimensions hold descriptions
Unique keys, single direction, full date table
Measures for anything that must respond to filters
Ratios: sum divided by sum, never averaged
